description.summary: A demonic, shape-shifting being of pre-Islamic Arabian and Islamic folklore, classed as a type of jinn, said to dwell in graveyards, deserts, and ruined places, lure travelers from their path, and consume corpses and human flesh.
description.full: The ghul (Arabic: غول, ghūl; feminine ghula/ghulah) is a demonic creature originating in pre-Islamic Arabian religion and continuing through Islamic folklore. Although the ghul is not named in the Qur'an, it appears in hadith literature, in pre-Islamic poetry, and across the wider Arabic and Persian narrative tradition, including 'One Thousand and One Nights'. In Islamic tradition the ghul is classed as a type of jinn — a being created from smokeless fire — that has chosen evil. Ghuls inhabit deserts, graveyards, and ruined places, and are said to lure travellers from their path, kill and devour them, prey on children, drink blood, and consume corpses. They are reputed shape-shifters, often appearing as a beautiful woman ('Mother Ghoul') or as a familiar relative; female ghuls are said to assume the form of the ghul's most recent victim. Pre-Islamic poets including Ta'abbata Sharra describe encounters and combats with ghuls, and Al-Mas'udi reports that the caliph 'Umar killed one in Syria. Al-Jahiz (9th century) was a major sceptic of the tradition, and the rationalist Mu'tazila school denied ghouls' existence outright. The English word 'ghoul' derives from ghul through Antoine Galland's French translation of the Nights and William Beckford's Gothic novel 'Vathek' (1786); H. P. Lovecraft and later authors recast it as a subterranean corpse-eating creature.

etymology.origin: Arabic غول (ghūl), from the root غ-و-ل / ghāla, 'to seize, snatch, attack unexpectedly'.
etymology.meaning: Literally 'seizer' or 'snatcher'; metaphorically a sudden calamity that destroys travelers.
etymology.first_use: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry (e.g. Ta'abbata Sharra, late 6th century AD); attested in English from 1786 (Beckford, Vathek).

related_phenomena.name: Djinn / Jinn
related_phenomena.description: Ghuls are classed as a type of jinn in Islamic tradition

related_phenomena.name: Jinn
related_phenomena.description: Same — broader category to which ghuls belong

related_phenomena.name: Ifrit
related_phenomena.description: Another powerful class of jinn in Arabic and Islamic tradition

related_phenomena.name: Marid
related_phenomena.description: Powerful class of jinn associated with the sea

related_phenomena.name: Vampires
related_phenomena.description: Blood-drinking, corpse-eating undead with cross-cultural parallels

related_phenomena.description: Cannibal monster of Algonquian folklore — shared cannibalism motif

related_phenomena.name: Gello
related_phenomena.description: Greek child-killing demon; argued by some scholars (Frank, Burkert, West) to share a Mesopotamian Gallû etymology with ghul

features.description: Can take the form of a beautiful woman, an elderly relative, or animals — often a hyena
In some traditions retains hoofed feet (e.g. donkey or hyena) when in human form, betraying its true nature
When unmasked, described as ugly, fanged, with claws and animal features
Often appears as a lone woman or 'mother' figure to lure male travelers
Said to take on the appearance of the most recently devoured victim

physical.morphology: Ghuls are described as inherently shape-shifters; their 'true' form is monstrous (fanged, clawed, animalistic), but they typically appear as humans (often women) or as animals (especially hyenas).

abilities.description: Takes human or animal form to deceive travelers
Calls to travelers, mimics familiar voices, leads them away from their path
Devours human flesh, including freshly killed victims and exhumed corpses
Said to drink the blood of victims
Uniquely among Islamic demons, ghuls are said to be capable of converting to Islam upon hearing the Throne Verse of the Qur'an

abilities.ability: Repelled by the call to prayer
abilities.description: Al-Damiri's hadith collection records that travelers can escape ghuls by reciting the adhan (call to prayer)

behavior.diet: Human flesh (living and dead), corpses, blood; in some accounts, also sheep and goats
patterns: Often appears as a woman ('Mother Ghoul') in distress to lure rescuers
Inhabits liminal spaces — desert, graveyard, ruin

range.description: The ghul belongs to Arab, Persian, and broader Islamic folklore. Reports and traditions extend across the Arabian Peninsula, the Levant, Mesopotamia, North Africa, the Maghreb, Iran, Afghanistan, and Central and South Asia, with regional cognates and equivalents elsewhere in the Islamic world.

hotspots.name: Arabian deserts

location.description: Wastelands and abandoned ruins of pre-Islamic Arabia; archetypal habitat in early poetry and hadith

hotspots.notes: Setting of the Ta'abbata Sharra ghul-combat poem and of 'Umar's reported encounter in Syria

first_recorded.source: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry attributed to Ta'abbata Sharra (late 6th century AD)

peak_activity_periods.description: Pre-Islamic poetry and early Islamic hadith, including reports by Al-Mas'udi and Al-Jahiz
Codification in Islamic literature (Al-Damiri's Hayat al-Hayawan, Al-Dimashqi) and incorporation in 'One Thousand and One Nights'

temporal.seasonal_patterns: No specific seasonal pattern documented; particularly associated with night travel through wilderness.

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Islamic Arabian religion and folklore. Possibly cognate with the Akkadian Gallû (an underworld demon) — a connection also proposed for Greek Gello.
origins.earliest_accounts: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry (late 6th century AD), including a poem attributed to Ta'abbata Sharra describing his slaying of a ghul; later doubted by Al-Jahiz.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely linked to the broader jinn complex of Arabic folklore and to wider Near Eastern traditions of corpse-devouring and child-killing demons (Lilith, Gello, Lamashtu).

timeline.event: Pre-Islamic poet Ta'abbata Sharra describes his combat with a ghul
Al-Mas'udi's later report that the second caliph 'Umar ibn al-Khattab killed a ghul with his sword while traveling in Syria
timeline.significance: Famous ghul-related anecdote in early Islamic historiography

timeline.event: Al-Jahiz (Kitab al-Hayawan) sceptically discusses the ghul tradition
timeline.significance: Earliest major rationalist critique of ghul belief

timeline.event: Al-Damiri's Hayat al-Hayawan ('Lives of Animals') records hadiths in which travelers escape ghuls by reciting the adhan
timeline.significance: Major medieval encyclopaedic treatment of the ghul

timeline.event: Antoine Galland's French translation of 'One Thousand and One Nights' (1704–1717) introduces ghuls to Western readers
timeline.significance: First sustained European exposure to the ghul tradition
timeline.source: Galland, Les Mille et Une Nuits

timeline.event: William Beckford publishes the Gothic novel 'Vathek', introducing 'ghoul' to English
H. P. Lovecraft's 'Pickman's Model' published, recasting the ghoul as a subterranean corpse-eating creature
timeline.significance: Basis for the modern Anglophone fantasy/horror ghoul archetype

history.modern_era: The ghul remains an active part of Arabic, Persian, and broader Islamicate folklore, periodically featuring in regional horror cinema (e.g. Egyptian and Saudi productions). In Anglophone popular culture, the post-Lovecraftian ghoul has largely displaced the original Arabic figure, especially in fantasy gaming (Dungeons & Dragons, Fallout) and horror fiction.

documentary.name: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry on the ghul
documentary.description: Body of pre-Islamic Arabic poetry describing encounters and combats with ghuls, including verses attributed to Ta'abbata Sharra.
documentary.analysis: Discussed and partly disputed by Al-Jahiz (9th century) in Kitab al-Hayawan.

documentary.name: Hadith literature on ghuls
documentary.description: Hadith collections and later commentaries (Al-Damiri's Hayat al-Hayawan, c. 14th century) preserving traditions of ghuls, their habits, and apotropaic recitations.
documentary.analysis: Standard medieval Islamic source-corpus for the ghul tradition.

documentary.name: One Thousand and One Nights
documentary.description: Multiple tales (e.g. 'The Story of Sidi Nu'man') feature ghuls and ghulas, especially women revealed as corpse-eating demons.
documentary.analysis: Vehicle for Western diffusion of the ghul through Galland's 1704–1717 French translation.
documentary.source: One Thousand and One Nights, various editions

paranormal.name: Ghul as a type of jinn
paranormal.description: Mainstream Islamic interpretation: the ghul is a real but invisible class of jinn, created of smokeless fire and morally responsible.

skeptical.name: Mu'tazilite / rationalist denial
skeptical.description: The Mu'tazilite school and Al-Jahiz argued that ghul stories are exaggeration, misperception, or poetic invention rather than reports of real beings.

skeptical.name: Folklore explanation: hyenas, brigands, and disorientation
skeptical.description: Modern scholarly explanation: ghul stories encode the real dangers of nocturnal desert travel — hyenas (which can scavenge corpses and laugh-call), brigands, and the disorientation of getting lost. The 1667 hyena attack at Mecca was locally attributed to a ghul.
proponents: Modern folklorists and historians of Arabic folklore
evidence_cited: Documented hyena scavenging in Arabian wilderness
Frequency of ghul stories along desert travel routes

traditions: Arabic and Persian folklore traditions of desert and graveyard demons
Apotropaic practices: reciting the adhan and Throne Verse to drive off ghuls
stories: Ta'abbata Sharra and the ghul (pre-Islamic poetry)
Caliph 'Umar's reported slaying of a ghul in Syria (Al-Mas'udi)
'The Story of Sidi Nu'man' and other ghul tales in One Thousand and One Nights
Persian Ghul-e Biyaban tales of Iran and Afghanistan
folklore.beliefs: The ghul is widely understood in Arabic and Islamic folklore as a real (though invisible or shape-shifting) jinn-class demon haunting deserts and graveyards. Apotropaic practices include reciting the adhan and Qur'anic verses, and avoiding solitary night travel through wild places.

literature: Antoine Galland (trans.) — Les Mille et Une Nuits (1704–1717)
H. P. Lovecraft — Pickman's Model (1927); The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath (1943)
other: Modern Arab popular culture: ghul as a stock figure in horror fiction and children's tales
